sections.summary: Introduces the paper's puzzle: applied time-series regressions often show high R2 and low Durbin-Watson d. It lists the consequences of autocorrelated errors, reviews stationary and integrated ARIMA representations, notes that economic levels are often near random walks or integrated processes, and presents simple random-walk and integrated-moving-average examples and benchmark forecasts.
sections.title: Spurious regressions and time-series background

source_span.end_text: TO examine this possibility, we conducted a number of simulation experiments which are reported in the following section.

sections.summary: Sets up the usual linear regression model with stochastic regressors, the null hypothesis, and the F test based on R2. It explains why autocorrelated residuals invalidate the test, discusses Kendall's variance result showing that high R2 can arise between independent autocorrelated series, and concludes that high R2 should not be treated as evidence of a significant relationship.
sections.title: Nonsense regressions in the standard model

source_span.end_text: is no indication of a true relationship.

sections.summary: Reports simulation experiments regressing independent random walks, finding inflated t-values and frequent false rejection of no relationship. It compares these results with Malinvaud's autocorrelation correction, extends the experiment to multiple independent regressors and different processes, and shows that random walks or near-random walks make spurious relationships the rule rather than the exception.
sections.title: Simulation evidence on spurious regressions

sections.summary: Concludes that strongly autocorrelated residuals imply mis-specification, whatever the observed R2. It considers possible corrections such as lagged dependent variables, differencing, or autoregressive errors, recommends first differencing highly autocorrelated variables, uses Sheppard's levels-versus-changes example, and discusses theory, lag structure, measurement error, and building models with both levels and changes.
